author_comment: All are reminders of the wonderful popularity of Adam in the north of England, if not in the south; cf. Adcock and Adkin, q.v. A common entry in the Hundred Rolls [of the 'fil. Ade' form]. With the variant Adice cf. Ellice for Ellis, or Bevance for Bevans.

record_text: 1713.—Edward, son of John Addis: St. Jas. Clerkenwell, ii. 71.

headword: Addyman
meaning: the servant or knave of Addy, i.e. Adam
author_comment: v. Addy and Addison. This is decidedly interesting. It is one of the chief witnesses to-day of the existence of the class of surnames to which it belongs. As a matter of course its home is in Yorkshire; cf. Mathewman, Peterman, Perryman, Jackman, Bartleman, &c. In the following entries, although Ade (i.e. Addy) is given as the nick. of Adam, the entry is unfortunately in Latin. In English it would have read Thomas and Johannes Addyman. We are more fortunate in a further instance, where the English form is given.
notes: souter (shoemaker); master of Johannes servicus Ade Symmeson
source: Poll Tax, West Riding of Yorkshire, 1379, p. 25
record_text: Adam Symmeson, souter, 1379: P. T. Yorks. p. 25.

headword: Adkin, Adkins, Adkinson, Atkin, Atkins, Atkinson, Atkyns, Adkisson
meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Addy, dim. Adkin, sharpened to Atkin
author_comment: There is no need of course to prove this, but it is interesting to note the following: 'Adam le Fullere,' a citizen of London, is twice referred to as Adekin le Fullere (1273, Hundred Rolls, i. 426). Six centuries ago Adam probably ranked as second or third favourite among boys' names throughout England. In the north it attained a most remarkable pre-eminence. Four Adams are mentioned in the revenues of Conishead Priory, A.D. 1256 (West's Furness, pp. 192, 195). No fewer than six Adams figure as benefactors of Furness Abbey, circa 1290 (ibid.). The everyday form was Adekin, then Adkin, and finally Atkin (see Addison). The following come together [Johannes Attekyson and Alicia soror Adekynson].
notes: Cited in the author's commentary; citizen of London; also called Adekin le Fullere
source: Hundred Rolls, 1273, vol. i, p. 426
record_text: 'Adam le Fullere,' a citizen of London, is twice referred to as Adekin le Fullere (1273, Hundred Rolls, i. 426)
